headline: Halfway Rock holds its cod, and the bass never left the ledges
subhead: Casco Bay's cool water keeps the daytime bite honest while points south go nocturnal — mackerel, bass, and groundfish all working on schedule.
body_markdown:
I was out past Jewell Island Tuesday morning, engine idling, watching a mackerel school dimple the surface off the eastern side of the ledge — hundreds of them, tight and nervous, with a dozen terns working the edge of the bait like they were grading papers. That's the kind of thing thirty years on this water teaches you to read before you even wet a line. When the mackerel bunch up that tight, something's pushing them, and it's usually bass or bluefish working from underneath.

Sure enough, ten minutes later, three keeper-class stripers came off the same ledge on small white bucktails bounced through the bait ball. Nothing heroic — twenty-eight, thirty, thirty-one inches — but steady, and taken in broad daylight at ten in the morning, which is worth noting. South of Cape Cod, in the warmer water, the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal this time of year, feeding under cover of dark because the surface temps in the low-to-mid seventies make daytime feeding thermally uncomfortable for them. Up here, Casco Bay is running cooler — mid-to-upper sixties on most days near the ledges — and that keeps our fish willing to work in daylight the way they always have. It's one of the real advantages of fishing this bay in August: you don't have to set your alarm for 3 a.m. to find them.

The ledge structure around Jewell, Cliff Island, and the back side of Great Chebeague has been holding bass consistently on the last two hours of the ebb into the turn — moving water pulls bait off the rocks and the stripers sit below, picking off what tumbles down. Small tins — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked on a slow retrieve through the current seam have been the most efficient producers, though live mackerel, when you can get one to stay on the hook long enough to fish it, still can't be beat as a livelining bait off these same drop-offs.

Halfway Rock continues to be the most dependable piece of structure in the bay for groundfish, and that hasn't changed from what I told you last week — I said then to expect little shift through the coming days, and that's exactly what's held. Cod and a few haddock are still coming off the deeper water on the northeast side of the Rock, in that eighty-to-hundred-and-ten-foot range, best worked on the slack around the turn of the tide when you can actually hold bottom without your jig sweeping sideways into the rocks. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly have been the go-to, dropped straight down and worked with a short, sharp lift-and-drop. It's not been a banner week — I'll be honest, some drifts produced nothing but a few cunner and a lot of patience — but on the days the tide cooperated, we put three or four keeper cod in the boat along with a haddock or two, which for early August groundfishing in this bay is a fair result.

Mackerel remain the most reliable fish in Casco Bay right now, and if you've got kids or a client who just wants bent rods, that's still the play. Schools are thick around Halfway Rock, off the southern tip of Peaks Island, and scattered through the mouth of the bay toward Two Lights. A string of small tinsel jigs, no bait required, dropped into a breaking school will load up fast — I watched a father-son team off Peaks fill a five-gallon bucket in under twenty minutes on Sunday. Use them fresh for bass bait that same day and you've closed the loop nicely.

Bluefish have been thinner up here than what's being reported to our south — the Jersey shore and the Sound are seeing a real push of blues right now, but Casco Bay hasn't seen much more than the occasional straggler mixed in with the bass off the outer islands. That's fairly typical for this water; the bulk of the bluefish push tends to stall out well south of us most years, and there's no strong signal yet that this year's different.

Down at Cape Small and off Bailey Island, the rips have been fishing best on the building tide — an hour either side of the flood seems to concentrate the bait against the ledges there, and bass have been sitting in the wash on the down-current side. Casting soft-plastic swimbaits, four to five inches, into the white water and letting them sink before starting a slow retrieve has worked better than burning them through — the fish there seem to want it presented like something struggling, not fleeing.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon over the next several days, and that means stronger tidal push through the bay's channels and around the ledges. I'd expect the groundfish bite at Halfway Rock to sharpen as the current strengthens and pushes more bait tight to structure — that's usually how it plays out here. If the wind stays reasonable, I'd put my time on the morning ebb at Jewell or Cliff Island for bass, and save the slack water windows for a drift over Halfway Rock's deeper structure. Patience pays on this bay in August. It always has.
